source.title: Towards understanding how momentum improves generalization in deep learning

record.file_problem: Text contains the paper and appendices; some figure values are not transcribed, and portions of table headers are garbled.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests when momentum changes generalization and reports settings where its benefit disappears or is reduced, refining any unconditional claim about momentum.
record.gate_note: The paper compares GD/GD+M and SGD/SGD+M on natural and synthetic datasets. Figure-only accuracies are recorded as such; table values are retained where the layout identifies them. Cited prior-work results are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study tests momentum versus no momentum, which none of V1–V8 names. Its batch-size sweeps report how momentum's advantage changes; the supplied text does not establish whether larger batches themselves lower accuracy under the fixed 300-epoch budget, and the plotted curves are unavailable. Its CNN/MLP comparisons use synthetic Gaussian inputs, not images.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors demonstrate conditional momentum benefits and prove a separation for a constructed shared-feature distribution: GD memorizes noise in small-margin examples, while GD+M continues learning their shared feature using historical gradients. They present this mechanism as a possible explanation, leaving its generality and interaction with stochastic noise open.
record.recipe_differences: Studies heavy-ball momentum versus no momentum, mostly with GD/SGD; it does not reproduce a listed original claim's method. Includes synthetic theory and experiments on VGG-19/Resnet-18.
record.method_sensitivity: The momentum benefit varies with batch size and is reduced by batch normalization and data augmentation; the Gaussian synthetic setting shows no consistent benefit.

fits_no_version.finding: Momentum improves CIFAR accuracy in several settings without augmentation or batch normalization; its advantage grows with batch size and is reduced by those training choices.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Heavy-ball momentum can improve held-out accuracy, depending on data structure, batch size, augmentation and batch normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Momentum improves classification of channel-shuffled small-margin images under full-batch training. Appendix A.5 also states that stochastic updates let SGD classify those images as well as SGD+M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Momentum's advantage on weak-feature examples depends on whether training uses full-batch or stochastic updates and on other regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Gaussian teacher/student experiments show no consistent momentum advantage. The constructed shared-feature distribution instead yields a theoretical GD/GD+M separation, corroborated by Figure 3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Historical gradients can improve learning of weak shared features in particular data distributions, without an unconditional generalization benefit.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 162, 2022
record.problems: Many key CIFAR results are presented only as plots without transcribed values. Table 1's header is garbled, preventing reliable assignment of most teacher/student pairs. The authors grid-search learning rates (and momentum parameter in the main experiments) for test accuracy, limiting inference about a fixed recipe.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted beyond results represented in figures as aggregate conditions; Gaussian Table 1 entries beyond the clearly aligned first pair could not be reconstructed from the supplied flattened header.

untested.parts: No fixed random-label fitting and held-out chance comparison.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison on image data or test of learned local connectivity.
No ascertainable large-versus-small-batch accuracy result in the supplied text; the reported momentum-benefit interaction does not establish the batch penalty or its removal.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or ranking of generalization gaps.
No influence-based identification and removal of memorized examples.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because no row measures a listed effect; this does not negate the momentum findings. Missing is empty because no additional ascertainable result tests a listed version. Table 1's headers are sufficiently readable to reconstruct its pairs. The paper also inconsistently labels Table 2(d) GD+M although the surrounding text identifies the stochastic momentum comparison.

versions.untested_parts: No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Compares momentum with no momentum, not adaptive optimizers such as Adam.
Varies batch size and reports how momentum's benefit changes, but does not state that large batches themselves have worse test performance than small batches under a fixed recipe.
Does not measure sharpness or other generalization measures.

rows.subject: VGG-19
rows.operation_detail: Compared GD test accuracy with and without momentum on artificially modified data.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10 with 10% randomly sampled images having shuffled RGB channels

rows.measure: Test accuracy; small-margin subset accuracy also reported
rows.note: Text gives small-margin accuracy drop factors: GD+M 79.47/53.30 = 1.49; GD 68.33/34.80 = 1.96.
rows.check: Measures momentum on channel-shuffled images, not random-label fitting or memorized-example removal. Split overall and small-margin accuracy: GD/GD+M are 68.33/79.47% overall and 34.80/53.30% on small-margin data. Figure 4 also specifies separately selected learning-rate schedules and weight decay.
